title: Vacuum and Autovacuum
subtopics: Why routine maintenance matters under MVCC
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Vacuum and Autovacuum.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to dead tuple cleanup.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Vacuum and Autovacuum. Its primary job is to help you operate a PostgreSQL instance by reading evidence from settings, logs, statistics, vacuum and storage tools. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing vacuum and autovacuum teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: operate a PostgreSQL instance by reading evidence from settings, logs, statistics, vacuum and storage tools. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

items.title: Dead tuple cleanup
items.text: Relate this point to vacuum and autovacuum: define the expected behavior, one edge case, and a query or check that would provide evidence.

items.title: The purpose of VACUUM
items.text: Use statistics and maintenance views to determine whether cleanup is working; do not disable automatic maintenance without a reviewed plan.

items.title: Autovacuum behavior
items.text: Use statistics and maintenance views to determine whether cleanup is working; do not disable automatic maintenance without a reviewed plan.

items.title: ANALYZE and statistics refresh
items.text: Read estimated rows and access paths first; when using EXPLAIN ANALYZE remember it executes the statement.

items.title: Why routine maintenance matters under MVCC
items.text: Identify the rows and transaction snapshots involved; test a second session and document blocking or retry behavior.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Vacuum and Autovacuum
content_blocks.code:
SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC NULLS LAST
LIMIT 10;
content_blocks.expected_output: Returns an approximate view of live/dead row estimates and recent autovacuum activity.
content_blocks.safety_note: Read-only query; do not disable autovacuum based on one observation.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run with permission to inspect the database statistics view. Stats are estimates and may be stale.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

content_blocks.title: Practical checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Maintenance checkpoint: monitor autovacuum and transaction age using evidence. Disabling maintenance without a reviewed plan can create serious operational risk.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Vacuum and Autovacuum”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “Dead tuple cleanup”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “Dead tuple cleanup”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Vacuum and Autovacuum, with an explanation of “Dead tuple cleanup”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Vacuum and Autovacuum fits into the broader goal to operate a PostgreSQL instance by reading evidence from settings, logs, statistics, vacuum and storage tools.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: Dead tuple cleanup, The purpose of VACUUM, Autovacuum behavior.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
